name: Anterior corticospinal tract
summary: The 10–15% of pyramidal fibers that do not cross in the medulla continue down the anterior funiculus beside the anterior median fissure as the anterior (ventral) corticospinal tract. Most of them cross at their segment of termination through the anterior white commissure to reach motor neurons of the trunk and proximal limb muscles, and some end bilaterally, so axial muscles have bilateral cortical control. This is why trunk and neck strength are relatively preserved in hemiplegia and why bilateral corticospinal lesions are needed to paralyze the trunk.

origin.note: Mainly from the trunk and proximal limb areas of the motor cortex and the supplementary motor area.

neuronChain.cellBody: Pyramidal cell in the motor cortex
neuronChain.synapse: on spinal interneurons and medial motor neurons after crossing in the anterior white commissure

decussation.level: Anterior white commissure at the segmental level
decussation.note: Uncrossed in the medulla; crosses segmentally, some fibers remain uncrossed.

waypoints.note: anterior funiculus beside the anterior median fissure, cervical and upper thoracic segments mainly
medial motor column via the anterior white commissure

termination: Medial motor neurons and interneurons of the cervical and upper thoracic cord for the neck, trunk and proximal limb muscles, bilaterally.

lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Little detectable deficit because of the bilateral projection
Loss of trunk control and postural stability with truncal weakness

pearls: Axial muscles have bilateral cortical control; unilateral strokes spare trunk and neck strength
The tract mostly ends in the cervical and upper thoracic cord and is often absent below
